name: Cinnabar/vermilion rouge

card.summary: Mercury sulphide pigment used historically in Rome, China and elsewhere to give the lips and cheeks a red colour.
card.aka: mercury sulphide rouge, vermilion, Tyrian vermillion
card.note: Contains mercury; poisonous, and not used in modern cosmetics.

quick.overview:
Cinnabar, the mercury sulphide mineral that gives the pigment vermilion, was used historically as red colour, including as a rouge-type cosmetic in the Near East and as cheek colour in Rome. The look it produced was a flush of pink to red on the cheeks, considered attractive and a sign of health.

Its toxicity was known in antiquity, and Roman sources treated mercury poisoning as an occupational disease. Modern cosmetics use other pigments.
quick.how: Historically powdered pigment applied to cheeks and lips. Modern makeup uses mineral and synthetic reds instead.
quick.risks: Mercury is toxic. Reviews describe cinnabar as poorly absorbed when swallowed but notes that heating releases mercury vapour. Long-term use may affect the kidneys.

lead: Cinnabar is mercury(II) sulphide, the historic source of the scarlet pigment vermilion.[1] It has been used as a colourant since antiquity in the Near East, including as rouge, and Roman women prized light pink on the cheeks as a sign of good health, with sources naming Tyrian vermillion among the rouges.[1][2]
For appearance, it gave lips and cheeks a vivid red or flushed look. Cinnabar and red lead were known to be poisonous but were still used extensively.[2]
Research on cinnabar concerns its toxicology and use in traditional medicine rather than cosmetic use, and no trial has tested it as makeup.

chain: Powdered cinnabar applied to cheeks or lips
angle.text: Cinnabar-based vermilion colored the cheeks and lips red, a look associated with health and beauty. It is documented as a historical cosmetic.

paras: Cinnabar has coloured objects since antiquity: Yangshao-culture stoneware in China, oracle-bone writing in the Zhou, and carved lacquer apparently from the Song.[1] Romans valued it as an interior wall paint.[1] As a cosmetic, it was used as rouge in the Near East.[1] Among Romans, light pink cheeks signified health and rouge sources included Tyrian vermillion.[2]

Mercury has no known physiological role in humans, and cinnabar and Chinese traditional medicines containing it have long been studied.[3][4] A review found cinnabar is insoluble and poorly absorbed from the gut, accumulating in the kidneys, while heating releases vapour that can produce toxicity like other mercury vapour.[4] The danger was recognised in Rome, where mercury poisoning was seen as an occupational disease, and miners at Almadén in Spain had shortened lives.[1]
No studies found on cosmetic use. Research on cinnabar concerns traditional medicines and mercury toxicity, including a review of cinnabar and realgar medicines.[4][5]

timeline.event: Cinnabar used as colourant and rouge in the Near East.[1]
Light pink cheeks fashionable; cinnabar and red lead used despite known poison.[2]
